class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Day 1 fans were ready for the journey. They sold out the show, proudly brandishing vintage “I Believe in Peace, B----” shirts (a lyric from 1994’s “The Waitress,” which Amos also nailed in the set). Grown men and women also shrieked when she pulled out rarer songs like a stunning gospel take of 1996’s “Way Down.” And the house gave Amos a standing ovation upon her first steps to the stage, before she even perched at her trusty piano.</p><p>There are music fans, and then there are Tori Amos fans — and over the course of nearly two hours, the beloved singer-songwriter delivered a show that activated her base and signed up any new members still on the fence. Even more remarkable, it’s all in spite of not playing her undying hits, “Big Wheel,” “Crucify” and “Cornflake Girl.” Indianapolis got that trifecta a few days prior, but Chicago got a mystifying “Winter,” a ghostly “Precious Things” and a rattling “i i e e e,” so, clearly, no complaints.</p><p>Amos has been mastering unique sets for each night of this current tour, which is a feat considering it requires the rapt focus of her backing ensemble, although they’re probably used to it by now. “We’ve been playing together forever,” Amos said, introducing musical director/vocal arranger/bassist Jon Evans and impeccable drummer Earl Harvin whose percussive wizardry and tribal thumps added to the ethereal mood of the night and allowed lots of space for Amos’ personality and vocals to fill. Helping her was a trio of “magical angel witches” on backup vocals, including Liv Gibson, Deni Hlavinka and Hadley Kennary, a Chicago native and graduate of New Trier. Their coordinated syncopation was downright stunning, evoking the alluring power of mythological sirens on the high seas.</p><p>There is one part of the Amos’ set, however, that has been repeated each night like ritual. It’s a mood-setting opener of “Fire to Your Plain” (2009) into the bold-new manifesto “Shush” from her latest album, “In Times of Dragons.” It’s a dark elegy that lambasts the silencing of women in the face of oppression and authoritarianism. In it, Amos calls out both the cursed prophet Cassandra and the modern heroine Courtney Love while also paying homage to the girl who wrote “Silent All These Years” long ago. Amos didn’t perform that number, but the message was still clear. Nearly 35 years after her groundbreaking debut, all the themes she wrote about back then — feminism, power, trauma, sociopolitics — are ever-relevant and there’s still work to be done.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7c0000" name="image-7c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0597f6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6642x3728+0+351/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2Fac%2F55dec5424aa19388af74295ac35e%2Ftoriamos-260817-07.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eae0f67/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6642x3728+0+351/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2Fac%2F55dec5424aa19388af74295ac35e%2Ftoriamos-260817-07.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e7f536c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6642x3728+0+351/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2Fac%2F55dec5424aa19388af74295ac35e%2Ftoriamos-260817-07.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Tori Amos performs at the Auditorium Theatre in the Loop, Friday, Aug. 14, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e7f536c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6642x3728+0+351/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2Fac%2F55dec5424aa19388af74295ac35e%2Ftoriamos-260817-07.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a159535/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6642x3728+0+351/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2Fac%2F55dec5424aa19388af74295ac35e%2Ftoriamos-260817-07.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e7f536c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6642x3728+0+351/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2Fac%2F55dec5424aa19388af74295ac35e%2Ftoriamos-260817-07.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Tori Amos performs at the Auditorium Theatre in the Loop on Friday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>That theme is the bedrock of “In Times of Dragons,” a concept album that Amos wrote (some parts with her twentysomething daughter Tash) as an allegory of the fight for democracy against tyrannical imposition. Friday’s show drove it home with curated imagery. As Amos barreled into “Shush,” the silhouette of a dragon appeared on a circular screen behind her, its claws moving, ready for a kill.</p><p>Yet, on later songs, as the proverbial heavy curtain lifted by the time Amos got to a defiant “God,” the circle became more of a mirror or looking glass for what a future could be if we perhaps learn from the truth speakers.</p><p>In these strange and harrowing times, the cultural coven has been activated. In recent months, feminist witches from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/04/11/review-florence-and-the-machine-allstate-arena-chicago-everybody-scream-tour" target="_blank" >Florence Welch</a> to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lollapalooza/2026/07/31/lorde-setlist-chicago-music-festival-lollapalooza-charli-xcx" target="_blank" >Lorde</a> have been invoking similar messages and casting their own spells on attentive audiences. While Amos may be a mother of the movement who opened the floodgates for the many transfixing singer-songwriters today, she wasn’t the first and she paid homage to one of her predecessors Friday.</p><p>The night wrapped with something “special” for Chicago: a rare performance of her 1992 B-side track, “Take to The Sky,” mixing in a bit of renegade Carole King’s “I Feel the Earth Move.” If there was any parting message, it was knowing that “In Times of Dragons,” it’s the ones who speak and sing with fire that have the power.<br><b></b></p><h3>Tori Amos set list for Aug. 14, 2026, show at Auditorium Theatre</h3><p>Fire to Your Plain<br>Shushi <br>i e e e<br>Bliss<br>Angelshark<br>Icicle<br>Way Down<br>Little Earthquakes<br>Sweet Sangria<br>God<br>Winter<br>The Waitress<br>Taxi Ride<br>Precious Things</p><p><b>Encore</b><br>Body and Soul<br>Take to the Sky</p>

entries.title: 2 wounded in Austin drive-by shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 50-year-old woman and a 20-year-old man were wounded in a shooting Friday morning in Austin, Chicago police said.</p><p>The man and woman were standing outside along the 400 block of North Pine Avenue about 9:37 a.m. when a dark-colored vehicle pulled up and someone inside fired multiple shots, police said.</p><p>The man suffered a gunshot wound and was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in good condition, police said.</p><p>The woman suffered gunshot wounds to her abdomen and left arm and was taken to the same hospital listed in critical condition.</p><p>No one has been arrested, police said. </p>

entries.title: Tyson Bagent didn't meet his own standard Saturday, but his value to Bears won't change
entries.summary: <p>When coach Ben Johnson first was asked about the possibility the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> might trade backup quarterback Tyson Bagent, he pretended to go into a coughing fit during the NFL Scouting Combine. He put his right hand to his mouth and let out an answer, emphatic and guttural.</p><p>‘‘No!’’ he said.</p><p>The preseason is the time when Bagent typically shows the rest of the NFL world what Johnson sees on the practice field and in meeting rooms.</p><p>As a rookie out of Division II Shepherd University in 2023, he beat out veteran P.J. Walker, to whom the Bears had just pledged more than $4 million. In 2024, he posted a preseason passer rating of 119.9. Last year, it was 106.6.</p><p>By comparison, his showing while playing the first half of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/15/bears-browns-soldier-field-preseason-score-10-tie-halftime-quarterback-tyson-bagent-nfl" target="_blank" >the Bears’ 34-10 victory</a> Saturday against the Browns wasn’t as flashy (13-for-22, 169 yards, 79.5 passer rating).</p><p>There wasn’t much for the Bears to be upset about as they walked off the soggy turf at Soldier Field. They committed only two penalties — Johnson wasn’t sure he ever had seen so few in a team’s first preseason game — and dominated the Browns in the second half en route to scoring the final 34 points.</p><p>But Bagent expected better from himself.</p><p>When Titans third-stringer Will Levis claimed this month that he was one of the best 32 quarterbacks in the NFL, many rolled their eyes. Bagent considers himself one of the best 32 and probably has a better case.</p><p>‘‘In order to be a successful quarterback in this business, you have to have an unrealistic confidence about yourself,’’ he said. ‘‘As far as I’m concerned, there was a lot of success in that first half, but there was also a lot of unacceptable things that took place. . . . If I am going to be one of those 32 guys, I’ve gotta play at a higher level.</p><p>‘‘Obviously, I’ve got to improve on that if I am going to be one of those guys in the near future.’’</p><p>That day will come — eventually.</p><p>Johnson valued Bagent so much that the Bears gave him a two-year, $10 million contract extension last year that kicks in this season. The money gave Bagent a more comfortable life, even if it came at the expense of delaying his starting-quarterback dreams for at least a year.</p><p>Bagent, 26, is more valuable to the Bears than he would be anywhere else, however. He’s wired like Johnson and is intensely obsessed with the position. He knows the offense inside and out. And he has proved to be proficient, at least in the preseason. As a rookie, he went 2-2 as a starter.</p><p>Bagent is what lets the Bears know they’re not one injury to Caleb Williams away from becoming the team that milled about on the visitors’ sideline Saturday. The Browns started Deshaun Watson, who posted a 98.2 passer rating and managed 10 points in his first NFL start in almost two years. Shedeur Sanders struggled in relief, and Dillon Gabriel was even worse.</p><p>Since the Bears drafted Williams No. 1 overall in 2024, he has yet to miss a meaningful snap. Bagent has taken only 27 snaps and thrown six passes in the last two seasons.</p><p>His opportunity, then, comes every August.</p><p>‘‘I’ve spent a lot of time on the sideline watching the game — the past two years, especially,’’ Bagent said. ‘‘So when my name is called upon, [I’m] able to give confidence to the coaches that I know what I’m doing and am able to be a coach on the field for these guys, be successful and keep the chains moving and put points up on the board.’’</p><p>In practice, Bagent often will criticize his own throws before Johnson has a chance to do so. On Saturday, he walked into Soldier Field wearing White Sox outfielder Brenton Doyle’s jersey — the two went to college together — and left wearing a hair shirt.</p><p>In the Bears’ preseason opener last year, Bagent went three-and-out on the first two drives before throwing a touchdown pass to wide receiver Maurice Alexander on the third. He vowed to start faster Saturday but went three-and-out twice before throwing a touchdown pass to Alexander.</p><p>‘‘Nowhere close to my standards,’’ he said.</p><p>In the second quarter, Bagent threw late over the middle to tight end Stephen Carlson and was intercepted by cornerback Michael Coats Jr.</p><p>‘‘Complete sloppy move on my part,’’ he said.</p><p>There were good moments, too. A 41-yard completion to wide receiver Kaden Davis on play-action to start the second quarter was Bagent’s longest pass of the game. And with 1:24 left in the first half, he engineered a 53-yard drive that ended in a 51-yard field goal by Cairo Santos at the gun.</p><p>Perhaps this offseason, some NFL team will watch Bagent’s film and make the Bears an offer they can’t refuse. In the modern NFL, every team with postseason aspirations needs a reliable backup quarterback, and the Bears have theirs.</p><p>‘‘You never know when a moment’s going to arise,’’ Bagent said. ‘‘So I think being able to attack each rep last it’s your last and really steward it the best you can is the only way to operate. That’s what I try to do.’’</p>

entries.title: Despite torrid stretch, Chase Meidroth isn't passing Colson Montgomery in lineup against righties
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — Colson Montgomery showed signs of life Saturday, capping a nine-pitch at-bat with a tiebreaking, two-run double in the third inning of the White Sox’ 4-3 victory against the Tigers.</p><p>Other than that, he struck out twice and flew out once, putting his batting average at .173 and his OPS at .541 since the All-Star break. Manager Will Venable batted Montgomery sixth in the order for the fifth time in the last six games to take pressure off of him.</p><p>Chase Meidroth also went 1-for-4, but it was very different. He had a hard-hit ball each time, defined by Statcast as a ball hit with an exit velocity of at least 95 mph. Meidroth’s exit velocity averaged 96.9 mph, and his second-inning single went off his bat at 99.3. It continued Meidroth’s torrid hitting since the break, which has seen him bat .326 with a .991 OPS.</p><p>Yet, Venable is hitting the right-handed Meidroth behind the left-handed Montgomery against righties. Why not move him up?</p><p>“There’s certainly a case for moving him up,” Venable said. “But you have to look at [our lineup] in totality. As you’re playing a team like the Tigers and you have A.J. Hinch, who’s going to do everything he can to match up, you have to be mindful of where guys are at. You can shift Meidroth up, but that allows for clean pockets for A.J. to hammer us with matchups.”</p><p>Before the series opener Friday, Venable said he experimented with Meidroth higher in the order in one of his half-dozen drafts. But he kept coming back to those pockets of lefties and righties for Hinch to exploit. Hence, Montgomery hit sixth and Meidroth seventh in Games 1 and 2.</p><p>But that doesn’t take away from the roll Meidroth is on. In his last 20 games, he’s batting .333 with a 1.063 OPS, five homers and 17 RBI.</p><p>“[He’s] hitting balls at better angles. More line drives,” Sox hitting coach Derek Shomon told the Sun-Times. “He’s obviously hitting more homers, but they’ve just been a byproduct of hitting balls hard at better angles, taking his shots and wanting to be aggressive inside of the at-bat.”</p><h3>Peters back in swing</h3><p>Tristan Peters is feeling good about himself again. Entering the Tigers series, he was hitting .177 in 29 games since the All-Star break. On Friday, he went 3-for-5 with a home run. He followed that up Saturday by going 2-for-4. It has been quite a relief.</p><p>“Felt like myself again; seeing the ball well,” Peters told the Sun-Times. “Honestly, you just got to ride the wave, avoid getting down on yourself. You’re going to have ups and downs. You’re not going to see the ball well. It’s a helpless feeling sometimes.”</p><p>Peters, whose pre-break performance made him an All-Star, said the adjustments he has made are more mental than anything.</p><p>“I found myself thinking about how my swing should be,” he said. “What I’m feeling as I’m in the box with my body. That gets me off my plan. But in the cage, we worked on staying on my back side a little more, staying behind the ball. [On Friday], it felt really good that I was able to see the ball for a lot longer.”</p><h3>Benny delivers vs. lefty</h3><p>It was very unlike Venable to let the left-handed Andrew Benintendi bat against Tigers left-hander Drew Sommers with the score tied at 3 in the seventh inning. But he already had pinch-hit with righty Randal Grichuk to begin the inning and was rewarded with a double.</p><p>Venable was rewarded again when Benintendi singled to left, scoring Grichuk for what held up as the winning run. The Sox increased their division lead to 4 ½ games.</p><p>“We only had a couple of bullets to fire there [righties Luisangel Acuna and Brenton Doyle on the bench],” Venable said. “Benny was going to get that at-bat against a lefty that was at the end of his day. entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson expects DE Montez Sweat, LT Braxton Jones ‘soon,’ but CB Kyler Gordon still 'unknown'
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> expects to have starting defensive end Montez Sweat and left tackle Braxton Jones within days. Nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon, meanwhile, is another story.</p><p>When asked how soon Sweat, who got hurt Aug. 6, would be back, Johnson was emphatic in saying, "Sooner, sooner, sooner, like within this week." The Bears will practice at Halas Hall on Sunday, Tuesday and Wednesday before a joint practice with the Bengals in Cincinnati on Thursday.</p><p>Johnson said the timetable on Jones, who got hurt the same day but already has been practicing in a limited capacity is, "Same thing."</p><p>Gordon is still on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list with a soft-tissue injury, and that's an ongoing frustration for the Bears. He missed 14 games with three different injuries last season, then got hurt in the recent offseason as well.</p><p>Johnson gave a one-word update on him: "Unknown."</p><p>Gordon has been around the team throughout training camp, but there's never been any clear projection of when he'll be back on the field. When pressed on that at the start of camp, general manager Ryan Poles didn't even commit to an expectation of him being back for the Sept. 13 opener at the Panthers.</p><p>The Bears already are down safety Coby Bryant, possibly for the season, and have uncertainty at outside corner with Tyrique Stevenson's inconsistent play. Cam Lewis originally was filling in for Gordon, but shifted to safety, then he got hurt. Newcomer Xavier Woods has been in that spot opposite rookie Dillion Thieneman lately.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Cubs, Matthew Boyd on wrong side of history in 8-4 loss
entries.summary: <p>Cubs ace left-hander Matthew Boyd came into Saturday’s game against St. Louis on a roll.</p><p>Cardinals left fielder Joshua Báez, making his major-league debut, slammed the brakes on it in – in historic fashion.</p><p>Báez homered in his first three at bats in the “bigs,” becoming the first player to ever do so – or go deep three times in his first game. St. Louis went on to top the Cubs 8-4 and dealt the North Siders only their third loss in their last 12 games.</p><p>All three of Báez’s drives, as well as Blaze Jordan’s sixth-inning home run, came off Boyd to match his career high for homers (four) allowed in a game.</p><p>“He hit three different pitches for home runs,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said. “He beat us for sure.”</p><p>Boyd, the Cubs opening day starter, entered Saturday 6-0 with a 2.43 ERA in nine starts since returning on June 25 from a stint on the IL for surgery on the meniscus in his left knee. But the Cardinals tagged him for seven runs on five hits and three walks in 5 1/3 innings and his record slipped to 8-2 with a 4.02 ERA.</p><p>Báez had been leading all Triple-A player in homers, with 34 in 101 games for Memphis. And the Cubs did have intel on the 23-year-old, rated as the Cards’ No. 2 prospect and the 56<sup>th</sup> overall by Baseball America.</p><p>“So we had a good idea,” Boyd said “I didn’t execute.</p><p>“Sometimes they’re (pitches) taken. Sometimes they’re good for singles or doubles, and he capitalized.”</p><p>Báez crushed the first major-league pitch he ever saw, Boyd’s 93.4 mph high fastball, 449 feet to center field for a two-run shot that gave St. Louis a 3-0 lead in the first.  </p><p>“Missed with the first heater and he was ready for it,” Boyd said.</p><p>The 23-year-old connected again in fourth, launching a solo shot to left on a low, full-count, changeup. That put the Cardinals back in front, 4-3, after Michael Conforto’s three-run arching shot down the right field line in the second had tied it 3-all.</p><p>“I thought it could have been a little more away and he put a good swing on it," Boyd said. </p><p>Báez’s smacked a two-run homer in the sixth to up the Cards lead to 6-3. This time the right-handed batter went “oppo” sending a slider on the outside edge of the plate to the front of the right-field bleachers.</p><p>“He hit a backdoor slider on the last one,” Boyd said. “That’s five runs from those three at-bats and that was the difference when it came down to it."</p><p>Jordan’s homer and a fifth St. Louis blast, by Alec Burleson off Colin Rea in the eighth, iced it.</p><p>Boyd yielded four homers in a game twice before, while with Detroit. Both contests were in August 2019, against Seattle and Minnesota.</p><p>Counsell said he didn’t see lot of mechanical difference in Boyd in this game, aside from a rocky first inning when he threw 24 pitches.</p><h3><b>Báez bio</b></h3><p>Báez is from Boston, but lived as kid in the Domincan Republic, before returning to Massachusetts at age 11. He had 30 family members and friends at Wrigley, including his mother</p><p>“For me to not only get a hit, but hit three home runs is just crazy,” Báez said.</p><p>He was just trying to stay calm before his first at-bat and look for a pitch “in his zone and be simple with it.”</p><p>And after the third homer?</p><p>“I was just really just glad that the ball just went over the wall and I had no idea (it was a record),”Báez said. “Then I saw it went over and I was like, 'This is insane' and like my teammates were so pumped up." </p><h3><b>Conforto connects</b></h3><p>Conforto’s 10<sup>th</sup> homer ended a 14-game drought, dating to July 21 versus Detroit.</p><p>He lofted a high fly at a 43-degree launch angle down the right field line. It landed just inside the foul pole.</p><h3><b>Dansby’s day off</b></h3><p>Shortstop Dansby Swanson didn’t start on Saturday, getting a routine maintenance day off.  </p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel entries.title: Bear down, Hammond Bears? At Soldier Field, fans didn't even want to hear it
entries.summary: <p>Bear down, Hammond Bears?</p><p>A smart-alecky reporter asked big-time fan Wlliam Garner, 42, of Burbank, if he was ready to sing those words Saturday shortly before kickoff of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ preseason opener against the Browns at Soldier Field.</p><p>Garner, with thick orange and blue chains around his neck and a Bears hat the size of a small Toyota on his noggin, met the idea with an “Oh, my God.”</p><p>“I’m just gonna say, ‘Bear down,’ ” Garner said. “Ain’t no place like Chicago.”</p><p>Andrew Ivinjack, son of a season-ticket holder, was enjoying a pregame beverage with lifelong pals Alan Checherz, Donovan Perry and Ethan Hunt. All four are in their mid-20s and hail from Lake Forest, though three now live in Lincoln Park or Lake View. Hunt was the most OK with the possibility of the Bears building a new stadium across the Indiana border, as long as it’s “truly state of the art.” The others, not so much. Perry called the very idea “disrespectful.”</p><p>“I would hate it if they built it in Hammond,” Ivinjack said. “How can you sing the fight song [about] ‘the pride and joy of Illinois’ if you’re in Indiana singing it? It just feels wrong.”</p><p>Bears chairman George McCaskey assured the public earlier in the week that fans would “adjust” to a stadium in Hammond if the team were to go that route. Checherz called that an “annoying comment.”</p><p>McCaskey and president/CEO Kevin Warren are pushing the idea of Hammond as the Bears’ “sole focus” among long-debated potential sites, which might not have the utmost truth to it considering they won’t rule out Arlington Heights, where the Bears are sitting on 326 acres.</p><p>If you said you were “solely focused” on the spiral ham Aunt Dotty just pulled out of her tote bag while not ruling out the 10-pound Wagyu prime rib roast you spent a fistful of hundreds on, it would be no less convincing.</p><p>Either way, “The time has come,” according to Warren, to move forward with a stadium that gives fans the “new environment and game-day experience” they deserve.</p><p>“I still love this experience,” said Ralph Peyton, 65, of Beverly, who was in the seats with brother Wayne Peyton, 63, and their cousin Keith Smith, 63, of Alsip. “I’m sure a new experience could be nice, but I appreciate this one.”</p><p>Of course, last season was a new game-day experience because the Bears were actually a good team, even beating the Packers twice on the lakefront. If the Bears went 6-11 in Hammond, in Arlington Heights or on board the International Space Station, that would be the old game-day experience.</p><p>McCaskey was in the broadcast booth as TV viewers got a look at images of the golf course — built atop a slag heap — at the proposed Hammond site. McCaskey pointed out that he could see the Chicago skyline in the distance.</p><p>Not the same thing, though.</p><p>“Where is the fan base in Hammond?” said Rich Zerillo, 44, of Mundelein. “There’s not much around there except for the casino, you know? So it’s kind of stealing away from the fan experience if they go to Indiana. It would be tough to stay a fan.”</p><p>Zerillo added that McCaskey “clearly is not in tune with his fan base if he thinks that people are just going to accept it.”</p><p>On fans’ first day at Soldier Field since the Bears’ board of directors voted in May to keep the Hammond train moving — at least for the time being — not all fans were bumming out. I’m going to have a hard time adjusting.”</p><p>When Lilianna Magana, 44, of Montgomery, south of Aurora, got wind of all this Indiana talk, she was “not happy at all.”</p><p>“You want to be on the lakefront and you want to be in the elements, right?” she said. “That’s what football is.”</p><p>Not that an Arlington Heights stadium would check those boxes, either, but at least it would be in Illinois.</p><p>“If it’s in the state of Indiana, I’m definitely not going to games anymore,” Magana said.</p><p>Zerillo is in the camp that believes the Bears are using the threat of moving to Hammond to leverage Springfield into giving the Bears the “tax certainty” they’re looking for to build in Arlington Heights.</p><p>“I’m not buying it,” he said. “It’s just a ploy.”</p><p>Garner lived eight years in Gary and another nine in Indianapolis</p><p>“I still wouldn’t want the Bears to go to Indiana. I’m going to be honest with you — not at all,” he said. “I wish they would just stay here. I love this area, love the atmosphere.
